extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students/scholars of poetics and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and theory for composing and evaluating dramatic and epic poetry (tragedy, comedy, dithyrambic, epic), focusing on imitation, meter, manner, and the elements that make poetic imitation effective and pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as the fundamental nature of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (fable) consists in imitation — a continued imitation (or narration) of actions; imitation is natural to men and is the principal cause of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetry as an art of imitation: choose actions to imitate and shape them so the audience can learn and take pleasure. The text argues imitation is innate and pleasurable, and that this natural desire is the starting point for poetic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal causes: Imitation and Number/Harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two principal causes that produced poetry: (a) imitation and (b) number and harmony (cadence, verse, song).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that imitation (what is represented) is united with suitable rhythmic/metrical structure. Imitation without number/harmony would not produce poetry, nor would number/harmony without imitation; both are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-fold distinction of imitation: With What, What, and How
rubrics_metrics.description: All imitation differs only in three respects — With What (the means), What (the subject), and How (the manner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, explicitly decide: the means (verse, singing, dance), the subject (which kinds of persons/actions), and the manner (narration vs dramatization). These decisions determine genre and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: narration vs acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitations may be made by narration (poet relates), by personation/acting (actors perform), or by a mixture; epics sometimes narrate or personate, dithyrambic poems are continuous narration, tragedies and comedies are action (actors) focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether the poem will 'remain the same' (narration) or 'make those act which we imitate' (drama). For theatre, rely on actors to embody action rather than poet's narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should represent great persons and actions (men better)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation of great persons' actions and represents them 'better' (greater, more elevated) than they are, while still making them somewhat like reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select noble/larger-than-life subjects and elevate their actions through poetic treatment; maintain likeness to human nature while heightening dignity and magnitude appropriate to tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy (old vs new): representation of the mean or likeness to life
rubrics_metrics.description: Old (mean) comedy represented men worse (exaggerated), whereas New Comedy endeavoured to make them like (more natural).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether comedy will caricature and lampoon (old/mean) or portray everyday life and characters realistically (new); the intended comedic tradition dictates tone and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of subject: actions (including terrible/horrible) can delight if well imitated
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may choose terrible or horrific originals (dead, dying, monstrous) because we behold them agreeably in imitation; the pleasure comes from the artful representation rather than from the fact represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shy away from grave or horrifying subjects; skillful imitation, arrangement, and presentation can produce pleasure and instruct the audience even with terrible material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure derives from artful presentation, not literal exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure we take in imitation does not come from exactitude of resemblance to the original (which most cannot judge) but from the art — the vivacity, mixture of colours (i.e., vivid craft), choice of action, posture, and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity, vividness, and artistic arrangement (diction, imagery, structure) over slavish literal accuracy when rendering events or characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate meter/number for function and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 'number' is included verse; certain meters suit certain functions: iambics are most proper for raillery and invective; hexameters/heroic meter for heroic/epic subject-matter. Trimeter and tetrameter usages evolved for dramatic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the meter to genre and tone: use iambic rhythms for sharp, conversational or invective passages; choose meters associated with solemnity or heroics for lofty material. Meter selection affects perceived suitability and character of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and evolution of dramatic devices (chorus, actors, songs, decorations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic form evolved (e.g., Aeschylus added a second actor, Sophocles a third; chorus songs were shortened; decorations, songs, and dance were integrated). These devices affect the gravity, motion, and spectacle of tragedy/comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When staging or composing drama, attend to the number of actors, the role and length of the chorus/choruses, incorporation of singing/dancing, and scenic decoration to achieve the desired blend of solemnity, movement, and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural composition: episodes, mixture and management of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of episodes and other beauties of tragedy were developed by degrees; Homer’s works are praised for admirable mixture of episodes, management of subject, nature of catastrophe, and episodic arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the structure (episodes/scenes) carefully to produce coherent progression toward catastrophe/resolution; aim for an artful mixture of parts (episodes, songs, choral odes) to create unity and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of poetic functions and suitable vocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets divided into those who composed hymns and panegyrics (more grave, lofty) and those who made raillery and invectives (lower, satirical). Different capacities and inclinations suit different poetic tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the mode (praise vs satire) that fits the poet’s capacity and the subject’s dignity; rigorous subjects demand loftier style and skill than lampooning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of instruction and delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation both instructs and delights; the pleasure of imitation invites learning and reflection. Poetry must engage understanding as well as senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for works that both educate (stimulate thought, understanding) and entertain (provide sensory/aesthetic pleasure) — craft should enable the audience to reason and be moved.
